grammar: # A bad token (#BD) the lexer hands the parser, and the error that ends a
# recovering parse: parsed by every runtime, fail-fast, under recovery and
# under relexing, and asserted field for field.
# FIVE tab-separated columns:
#   grammar  `json`, or the name of an `# @grammar` definition below
#   opts     serialized engine options, installed as a second grammar
#            carrying nothing but `options`, or `-` for none; or the word
#            `continuations`, and the row asks the engine what could
#            follow the input (`continuations(input)`) instead of parsing
#            it: `value` is then the token names it answers, in its order,
#            joined by `,`, and `errors` is `-`
#   input    the source; \n, \r and \t are decoded, as in every file here
#   value    the parse result: `-` when a fail-fast parse throws, else the
#            value in the shared canonical form (map keys sorted, and an
#            absent value -- TS undefined, Go nil, Rust None -- as `null`;
#            DIVERGENCE.md "A parse that sets no value")
#   errors   `-` for none, else every error, in order, as `code@row:col`,
#            with the recovery metadata the engine attached to it:
#            `+bad<n>` for a bad token recorded at fetch time as a run of n
#            tokens, `+skip<n>` for a recovery that skipped n tokens to its
#            sync token, and nothing for an error the parse ended on
#            unrecovered. A fail-fast parse lists the error it threw.
# `json` is ts/test/json-builder.fixture.json, the serialized strict-JSON
# grammar all three runtimes already load, installed on a default engine
# with `rule.start` set to `val`. Every grammar here runs with ONE custom
# lex matcher, which each runner builds natively because a serialized spec
# cannot carry code, and which must behave identically in all three:
#   name `bad`, order 1.5e6 (after `match`, before `fixed`). At `?` it
#   returns a bad token with why `custom_bad` whose source is the `?`; at
#   `%`, one with why `custom_unterminated` whose source runs to the end of
#   the source; at `!`, one whose source is the `!` with NO why and its err
#   set to `custom_err`, the shape TS `Token.bad`, Go `Token.Err` and Rust
#   `Token.err` give a token a matcher builds itself. None advances the
#   cursor, as TS `lex.bad`, Go `lex.Token` on the cursor and Rust
#   `Lexer::bad_span` do not. Anything else it declines. First, though,
#   at the very start of the source it steps over a U+FEFF, one character
#   and one column, and carries on from there in the same call, as the
#   xml plugin's matcher steps over a byte-order mark: so a mark it steps
#   over and nothing after it leaves the cursor at the end of the source
#   with nothing matched.
# The canonical engine raises such a token the moment it is fetched, with
# its own code at its own position; under recovery it records it,
# coalesces a run of them into one error, and steps past it; under
# relexing it leaves it in the lookahead for an alternate to re-cut. The
# check for content after the parse raises it without recording it first.
# A recovering parse that gives up lists every error once: the one it
# gave up on is the last one it recorded, or a cascade it dropped.
# The code of a bad token is its why, else `unexpected`. err is not read
# where a rule fetches the token, nor where the trailing-content check
# meets it (ts/src/rules.ts, `tkn.why || UNEXPECTED`), so a token with
# only err set is `unexpected` there. err is read, ahead of why, only
# where recovery is attempted after every alternate declined the token
# (`tkn.err || tkn.why`), which relexing with recovery reaches. Go once
# gave such a token's fail-fast error no code at all, and read its err
# under recovery and in the trailing-content check (#267).
# ts/test/bad-token.test.js and rs/tests/bad_token_fetch_test.rs pin the
# rows under "Relexing with recovery", the cascade at the cap and the
# continuations after a complete document a second time, as the canonical
# engine's own statement of them: Go once answered each differently.
# Runners: ts/test/bad-token.test.js, go/bad_token_spec_test.go,
# rs/tests/bad_token_spec_test.rs.

# @grammar nest {"options":{"rule":{"start":"top"},"fixed":{"token":{"#LB":"<","#RB":">"}}},"rule":{"top":{"open":[{"s":"#LB","p":"body"}],"close":[{"s":"#RB"}]},"body":{"open":[{"s":"#NR"}],"close":[{"s":"#RB","b":1},{"s":"#ZZ","b":1}]}}}
#   `top` reads `<`, pushes `body` and closes on `>`; `body` reads a number
#   and closes on `>` or the end, leaving either to its parent.
# @grammar one {"options":{"rule":{"start":"top"}},"rule":{"top":{"open":[{"s":"#NR","a":"@value$"}]}}}
#   One number, and nothing to close: the parse loop ends without reading
#   past it, so what follows meets only the trailing-content check.

#   One number or one text token, and nothing to close; the rows switch
#   the text matcher off with `{"text":{"lex":false}}`.
# Fail-fast. A bad token is raised where it is fetched, with its own code,
# whichever position of an alternate asked for it.
